blocks.p: From Lagrange One, Stephen had told him, the Earth was the size of a coin held at arm’s length.

Sol saw it that way first, through the small thick port of the Mercy Office ship, when the pod opened and the warmth came back into his hands and a warden in white helped him sit up. A coin, blue and white, very far off. He watched it for an hour while the ship came in, and it grew, as Stephen had never seen it grow, until it was the whole of the port, a great curve of blue with the clouds lying on it in long combed drifts and the sunlight coming off the sea so bright he had to look away.
He had not seen it in thirty-two years, nor, he realized, thought about it in nearly as long. On Philippa the Earth was a word in the liturgy that he no longer said.

Lyda was in the next seat, her hand behind her left ear, where Lucan’s coin sat under the skin, waiting for her head to clear; she always came out of the cold slower than he did. When it cleared she leaned across him and looked out without a word for a long time.
“So that’s it,” she said at last.
“That’s it.”
“It’s very blue.” She considered it. “I thought it would look older.”

He looked at the sea, wide and calm and shining under the cloud, and tried to find on it some sign of what the Remembrance said had been done to it, a third of it made blood, a third of everything in it dead. There was nothing. The sea had closed over the place long ago, as the crowd had closed over the place in the Bounty Market where an old man had fallen. Somewhere down there, Stephen had said, a light no bigger than a pinprick had gone out on the night side.
A third of the sea became blood. He did not say the response. He found he was holding Lyda’s hand.
Earth was lighter than Philippa.

He had not expected that. He came down the ramp of the ship onto the white stone of the landing field at Sion with a warden at each elbow, braced for the weight of the home world, and it was not there; after thirty years of Philippa’s pull his legs found the Earth easy, almost buoyant, and his knees did not hurt. It felt like a kindness he had not earned, and he distrusted it at once.
The city began at the edge of the field and did not end.

He had lived in it for most of four hundred years. But he had forgotten, or never seen, how it went on: white towers and white terraces stepping away toward the horizon in every direction, gardens hanging from every level, bridges of pale stone running between the towers high in the air, and on every one of them, people. Billions of them. The air over Sion was full of their sound, a soft enormous murmur like the sea heard from a long way off, and under it, from nowhere in particular, music.
And everywhere, the Pearls.

He had forgotten that too. In the colonies a Pearl was a thing in a house or a church, a door in a wall. In Sion they were everywhere the eye fell. There was one at every corner of every street they passed through in the closed car, and one in the car itself, set into the partition behind the driver, glowing its deep patient gold. People stopped at them on the street the way people in Abundance stopped at fruit stalls. Sol watched a young man in a fine coat pause at a corner Pearl, touch his temple, and speak to it briefly, smiling, the way one gives an order to a servant one likes, and walk on. A woman knelt at another with two children beside her, all three with their hands open on their knees. At a third a whole queue waited patiently, each one stepping up in turn, asking, thanking, stepping away. The light warmed for every one of them.
“What are they asking for?” Lyda said.
“Everything,” Sol said.
There were no old faces.

He looked for one. He could not help it. In all those thousands of faces there was not one line, not one white head, not one stoop. They were beautiful. Every face was smooth and handsome and about thirty, or about forty, as the fashion was, and content, and every one of them, when the car stopped at a crossing and the wardens helped him out to walk the last of the way to the house of the Mercy Office, turned toward him and went still.

He had felt it in the Long Gallery on Serenity. Here it was a hundred times worse. The crowd at the crossing drew back from the two old people in their colonial coats the way water draws back from a stone, and the murmur died around them in a widening ring, and in the silence a child said clearly, “Mother, are they denied?” and her mother did not answer, but put her hand over the child’s eyes.
Lyda looked straight back at all of them. She had a way of looking at a crowd as if it owed her money.
“They’ve done well for themselves,” she said, loud enough to carry.

The room they were given was very high up in the house of the Mercy Office, and it was not a cell. Sol had expected a cell. It was a white room with a soft wide bed, a table set with fruit, a long window over the city, and warm water that came when it was asked: the most comfortable room he had been in for thirty years. The door did not lock from the inside.
In the wall opposite the bed, set into an alcove no larger than a door, there was a Pearl.

Lyda stood and looked at it a while, with her hands in her coat pockets. Then she took her coat off and hung it over the Pearl by the collar, carefully, so that it covered the whole pane, and smoothed it flat, and went to wash.
The gold showed at the edges all the same, a thin bright line around the dark cloth, like light around a door.
Toward evening someone knocked, and the door opened, and a deacon came in with a tray.

He set it on the table: bread, a covered dish, a pot of tea, two cups. He was a slight man in the grey of a house deacon, neat and quick, with a pleasant smooth face and the manner of someone who has always been glad to do exactly what he was asked. He straightened and turned to bow to the guests, and Sol saw his face, and could not for a moment breathe.
“Remember the Mountain, sir,” Pell said.

He had not changed. It was the same face that had come up at Sol’s elbow in the Bounty Market with the morning’s tablets, and stood in a corridor on Concord holding a packed case because it did not know what else to do. Thirty-two years had gone over it like water over glass.
“Hello, Pell,” Sol said.
The deacon’s pleasant face went still. “I’m sorry, sir. Have we met?”
“A long time ago.”

“I’m afraid I meet a great many people in the house.” Pell smiled apologetically. “You’ll forgive me.” He lifted the cover from the dish, and steam came up, and he set out the cups. Then he stopped, with the teapot in his hand, and looked at Sol again, more carefully, as if something in the face had caught on him.
“You have a look of someone,” he said. “A bishop I served once. In the colonies. Bishop Tarren.”
“What happened to him?”

“He went away.” Pell poured the tea. His hands were perfectly steady. “He was ill, I think. I was told he was ill. I always thought he’d be back.” He set the pot down. “I asked to be posted to this house, you know. I don’t quite know why. I had a very good place at Concord. I think I thought...” He frowned slightly, the way he had frowned once over the stain on his own sleeve. “I thought I’d like to be where the people come in.”
“Are you happy, Pell?”

“Oh, yes, sir. Always.” He said it simply, as a fact about himself. He looked at Sol’s hands on the table, at the tremor in them, and his face softened. “It gets cold in the house at night for... for older guests, I’m told. I’ll bring another blanket.”

He brought it. He laid it across the foot of the bed and smoothed it with exactly the care he had once given Sol’s folded stoles. Then he straightened, and his right hand came up from his side and went toward Sol’s shoulder, toward the place where a stole would have lain, the fingers already shaped to set a fold straight. It reached the rough colonial wool of Sol’s coat and stopped there, and rested a moment, and did not seem to know what it had come for. Pell looked at it. Then he took it back and put it behind him with the other, and went to the door, and turned there, and began to bow: not the small nod a house deacon gives a guest, but the other one, from the waist, the one he had made at the study door every morning for sixty years. Halfway down it stopped, as if the rest of it had been mislaid. He came up slowly.
“Remember the Mountain, sir.”
“Goodnight, Pell,” Sol said.
Pell had the door half closed. He stopped.
“I didn’t tell you my name,” he said.
“No.”

The deacon stood in the doorway a moment longer, with his hand on the frame. Then he lifted his other hand and touched the corner of his own eye with one fingertip, and looked at the fingertip, and found it dry. He smiled at them both, vaguely and kindly, and closed the door.
Lyda said nothing for a while. Then she poured the tea, and put a cup into Sol’s hands, and closed his fingers around it with her own, and held them there until they had stopped shaking.

Aurelian came late, long after the city’s bells had rung the last office. He knocked very softly, and when Sol opened the door he stood in the corridor in his white robes with his hands at his sides and did not come in.
“They said I might,” he said. “If you’ll let me.”
Sol stood aside.

Aurelian came in and looked at the room, at Lyda sitting up in the bed with a blanket around her shoulders, at the coat hung over the Pearl with the gold showing at its edges. Something moved in his face at that. Then he went to the wall beside the window and sat down on the floor with his back against it and his knees drawn up, the way he had told Sol once, on a sealed line long ago, that he had sat on the floor of his rooms for an hour.
Sol lowered himself into the chair across from him. It took him a while.

“I want to tell you the rest,” Aurelian said. “I said I would. In the water.” He looked at his hands. “They didn’t send me. I want you to know that, whatever else you know. They came to me after someone noticed I’d been reading Weir’s registry, and asked me why, and I told them. They were so kind about it, Tarren. They said I could bring you home. They said you were old and ill and a long way off, and you’d die out there with no one to receive you, and wouldn’t it be a mercy.” He swallowed. “And I believed them, and I didn’t, both at once, the way you believe things in Sion. And I asked to go. I asked.”
“And the water?”

“I meant the water.” He looked up, and his eyes were dry and terrible. “I meant it all the way from Sion to Philippa and all the way back. And I signed the order. I want you to have both. They gave it to me in Sion to carry, finished except for a bishop’s hand. At Plenty the packet waited two hours for clearance, with you and your wife already under the lids, and I sat in the lounge at the evening office and signed it. I told myself I’d void it after the water. I’d go in and come up dark and void it, and no one would ever know.” He drew a breath. “I stood in the water this morning up to my knees and thought, now, do it now, before he comes, and walk up the stair to him already done. And I couldn’t. And then I heard them come in behind the pumps, and then you came down the stair, and I felt...” He stopped. “I was glad. That’s what I came to tell you. When I knew they were there, I was glad. It was over, and I didn’t have to choose anymore.” His face twisted. “As if I hadn’t chosen at Plenty, with my own hand, while you slept. That was the lie, Tarren. Not the water. The water was true. The lie was that there was still anything left to choose.”
Sol said nothing. Across the room Lyda had not moved.

“And the Petrel,” Aurelian said. “I was told something would be arranged for you at Galatia. Quietly. They can’t send wardens past Plenty, so they arrange things, through whatever hands are there already. That’s what I was going to say on Philippa. I asked for your road to be changed, so you wouldn’t go to it. I thought I was saving you. That’s all I know.” His voice thinned. “I’ve tried for thirty years to remember whether I knew what the other road would be. Whether anyone told me about the Scatter, and I let them. I can’t find it. I don’t know anymore whether I can’t remember or won’t.” He laughed, very softly. “Lucan would have written that down.”
“He did,” Sol said. “In a way.”

“Here is the last thing.” Aurelian drew his knees up tighter. “I go under in the autumn. The east hall. I’ve put my name down for a full curation. There’s a form; they’re very gentle about it. I’ve asked them to take it. All of it. The registry. The river. Your face on the stair.” His mouth moved. “You. I’ll wake up and you’ll be a friend who went away, a long time ago, somewhere far off, and I’ll be sorry about it in the ordinary way. The way one is sorry about weather.”

Sol thought of the steps of the east hall in the morning light, the honey cakes coming out on a tray, Aurelian’s arm round him, and the two of them saying it together like a response. Not anymore. It had been the best joke in Sion. He understood now what it had been all along.
“Don’t,” he said. “Aurelian. You’ll come out in the autumn and sit down on those steps by yourself, and if anyone ever tells you about me, you’ll laugh and say not anymore. And it will be true.”
“That’s the mercy of it. You don’t know what it is, carrying this.”

“I know exactly what it is.” Sol leaned forward in the chair, hard, and did not care what it cost him. “I signed for Stephen. I signed for thousands. I carry every one of them. It’s the heaviest thing I’ve ever lifted, Aurelian, and it is the only thing I own that they couldn’t touch. Don’t give them the one thing in your head that’s still your own.”
“It’s not a thing. It’s a wound.”

“Then let it be a wound.” Sol’s voice shook. “I told you once about the man by the fire, the one who said three times he didn’t know him. You remember what he did when the cock crowed. He didn’t go and have it taken out. He went out and wept. That’s the way back. It’s the only one I know of. Forgetting isn’t a way anywhere.”

“I can’t.” Aurelian’s voice broke, and still his eyes were dry. “Don’t you think I’ve tried? I sat on the floor again, after Serenity, for three hours. Nothing comes, Tarren. They’ve taken out the place where it comes from. They took it out a long time ago, and I let them, and I thanked them for it.”
“It came for me late,” Sol said. “On a packet. In the dark. I didn’t go looking for it.” He held out his hand. “Say his name. Here. Now. Once.”
Aurelian looked at the hand. For a long moment Sol thought he would take it.
“I can’t,” he said. “Say it to me.”

In thirty years no one had asked Sol for the name who did not mean to follow it into the water. He said it anyway, quietly, across the small white room, the way he had said it in a hundred small rooms: “Christ.”
Aurelian did not move. His eyes went to the corner of his sight, where the forms waited, where everything he heard went up the line; and then, deliberately, back to Sol’s face. “Again,” he said.
Sol said it again.

Aurelian shut his eyes on it, the way a man shuts his mouth on something too hot to hold, and kept them shut, and Sol watched him not let it go. Then he got up off the floor, slowly, like a much older man, and smoothed his white robes, and his face closed over again like water over a dropped stone.

“The Hierarch has asked to see you,” he said. His voice was nearly his own again. “In the morning. He asked for you himself; he’s never asked for a prisoner in his life. He’s curious. He said...” The ghost of the old amusement crossed his mouth and was gone. “He said he’d never met a man who stopped.”
He went to the door. He did not look at the coat over the Pearl.
“Aurelian.”
“Don’t,” Aurelian said, very quietly, with his back to them. “Please. Don’t forgive me again. I can’t bear it.” And he went out.
Lyda lay down after a while, and turned on her side toward the wall. Sol thought she was asleep. Then she said, into the dark, “He’ll do it.”
“Perhaps.”
“He’ll go under and wake up and smile at you in a corridor. Like the deacon.”
“Perhaps,” Sol said again. “I’ll pray anyway.”

He knelt by the bed, because he could not have got down onto the floor and up again, and put his forehead on the blanket Pell had brought, and prayed for Aurelian by name. He’s afraid. He was always the one who was afraid. Find him. Ask him three times. Ask him a hundred times. Don’t let them take it. Then, because he was learning not to leave anyone out, he prayed for Pell, who was happy, and for the child at the crossing with her mother’s hand over her eyes.

When he lifted his head the room was dark except for the Pearl. Lyda’s coat hung over it, still and black, and all around its edges the gold burned on in a thin unwavering line, patient, like light around a door that someone on the other side was waiting to open.
